audits.claim: R4 row: the term and construction come from PS75's cross-referenced 'Clavus Latus' entry (pp. 293-294): a broad purple band woven down the centre of the tunica; the stripe marks the senatorial order while the narrow stripe marks the equestrian order.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/synthesis/costume-language-coupling-table.md:82 (R4 row; also line 12 source key PS75)
audits.source_locator: Anthony Rich, 'Clavus Latus, Clavus Angustus', in William Smith, A Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities (John Murray, 1875), pp. 293-294; opening paragraph and the Pliny citation sentence; page markers p293 and p294 both present in the transcription
audits.source_excerpt: it is now established beyond doubt that the clavus latus was a broad purple band, extending perpendicularly from the neck down the centre of the tunica ... These purple stripes were woven into the tunic
audits.basis: Word-for-word correspondence for breadth, colour, placement (down the centre of the tunica) and weave; the same page calls the latus clavus 'a distinctive badge of the senatorian order' and the angustus clavus 'the decoration of the equestrian order', which is the coupling the row asserts. Page range in the entry matches the transcription header (pp. 293-294).
audits.access_limit: Public-domain 1875 transcription inspected; the printed volume itself was not consulted, and no modern re-assessment of the clavus-reconstruction debate was retrieved in this pass.

audits.claim: R4 row: senatorial association, but Augustus also permits senators' sons to wear the stripe after the adult toga (SA 38.2), and that passage names the stripe only, not its fibre or weave.
audits.source_locator: Suetonius, The Life of Augustus, ch. 38, sentence 2 (John C. Rolfe trans., Loeb Classical Library, 1914; Thayer transcription)
audits.source_excerpt: To enable senators' sons to gain an earlier acquaintance with public business, he allowed them to assume the broad purple stripe immediately after the gown of manhood and to attend meetings of the senate
audits.basis: The retrieved sentence supports both halves of the row: the wearers are senators' sons, and the stripe is assumed with the toga virilis ('immediately after the gown of manhood'). It names the stripe alone, consistent with the entry's own hedge, so the entry's wording is neither over- nor under-stated.
audits.access_limit: English translation inspected only (Latin text not read). Counterweight recorded, not a contradiction: Rich (1875), p. 294, frames such grants as a personal indulgence also extended to children of equestrians (citing Ovid, Trist. IV.10.29); that qualifies how general the Augustan grant was, not what the entry claims.

audits.claim: R3 row and source key: PS75 records pura/libera for the adult white toga and cites Ovid, Fasti III.771 for libera; the coming-of-age association with the Liberalia is a literary association, not proof of ceremony date.
audits.source_locator: Philip Smith, 'Toga', in Smith's Dictionary (1875), p. 1137 (page marker p1137 present)
audits.source_excerpt: The colour of the toga worn by men (toga virilis) was generally white, that is, the natural colour of white wool. Hence it was called pura ... The toga virilis is called libera by Ovid (Fasti, III.771).
audits.basis: The p. 1137 text carries exactly the two lexical claims the entry attributes to it, including the Fasti III.771 citation for libera; the entry already scopes the Liberalia link to Ovid's literary account rather than a dated practice.
audits.access_limit: I did not re-inspect the Kline or Loeb Ovid text in this pass; the entry's own Ovid/Loeb check is not independently re-verified here, and the Ovid coupling remains attributed-literary.

audits.claim: Q1 row: 補子 buzi is the standard modern/museum citation form for the Ming-Qing object type (cited to Cleveland and Kyoto National Museum records).
audits.source_locator: Cleveland Museum of Art open-access record 1985.32, title and description fields; same title form 'Rank Badge (buzi)' on 1948.69, 1948.71, 1948.72
audits.source_excerpt: Rank Badge (buzi) ... Rank badges (also called rank insignia or Mandarin squares) were used in China during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties to demonstrate the wearer's rank.
audits.basis: An institutional catalogue uses the romanised form 'buzi' as part of the object title for Ming- and Qing-period badges, which is what the entry claims about modern/museum citation practice.
audits.access_limit: Cleveland records were read through the public open-access API, not the gallery pages; the Kyoto National Museum records the entry also cites were not retrieved in this pass, so that half of the citation remains located-only.

audits.claim: Q1 row: the crane-first-rank pairing is reported from the 1391 Ming insignia regulation in exhibition cataloguing; the rank reading is a curatorial reading, and period regulation text and exceptions remain open.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved-json (Cleveland regulation sentence); Met interpretive text NOT retrieved
audits.source_locator: Cleveland 1985.32 / 1948.69 description paragraphs ('In 1391 ...'); divergent rank statements in 2019.78.1, 2019.78.2 and 2020.259 descriptions
audits.source_excerpt: In 1391 new clothing regulations directed court officials to wear decorative squares indicating their rank-birds for civil officials and animals for military officials.
audits.basis: The 1391 regulation and the bird/animal principle are supported as an exhibition-catalogue report, but no retrieved text states that the crane was the first civil rank: Cleveland's crane badges are described as 'fourth or higher ranks' and one portrait's crane as the 'third ranked officer'. The entry's hedges ('curatorial reading', 'reported from ... exhibition cataloguing') are therefore doing real work; the marker stays open and nothing is cleared.
audits.access_limit: Metropolitan Museum object page text for 30.75.830 / 36.65.10 could not be retrieved (page requests rate-limited; the archived snapshot exposes metadata fields only, no crane-rank sentence), and no Ming regulation text was obtained. Rank-specific retrievals beyond Cleveland were not available in this pass.

audits.claim: M1/M2 object metadata: M1 catalogued to the Kangxi period 1662-1722 in silk and metallic-thread tapestry (kesi); M2 dated only to the late seventeenth-early eighteenth century, embroidery on silk satin.
audits.source_locator: The Met Collection API, objects 60511 (accession 30.75.830) and 62893 (accession 36.65.10): title, period/objectDate, medium, accessionNumber
audits.source_excerpt: Qing dynasty (1644-1911), Kangxi period (1662-1722) ... Silk and metallic thread tapestry (kesi) ... late 17th-early 18th century ... Silk and metallic thread embroidery on silk satin
audits.basis: The retrieved API records reproduce every metadata attribution the entry assigns to M1 and M2, including the different precision of the two datings (period 1662-1722 for M1, century-range only for M2).
audits.access_limit: Structured API metadata only; the museums' interpretive catalogue prose was not retrieved, and museum records are mutable, so these attributions are dated to 2026-10-17.
